data.title: Sudo Configuration Permits Privilege Escalation
data.summary:
Sudo rules granted standard users the ability to run commands that provide a shell escape
or write arbitrary files, allowing escalation to root beyond the intended scope of the
rule.
data.description:
Sudo rules are written to express intent — "this user may restart this service" — but are
enforced as "this user may run this binary as root". Where the binary can spawn a shell,
read or write arbitrary paths, or load a user-controlled configuration, the rule grants
root.

Editors, interpreters, archive tools and anything with a shell escape all fall into this
category, and many are granted routinely because the operational need is genuine.
Wildcards make it worse, since an argument the author did not anticipate frequently
satisfies the pattern.

Credential caching extends the exposure: a session that has recently authenticated can be
used without re-prompting, so compromising a session is sufficient.
data.recommendation:
* Review sudo rules against the actual capability of each permitted binary rather than
  against the intent of the rule.
* Avoid wildcards; enumerate the permitted invocations explicitly.
* Use purpose-built wrapper scripts with fixed arguments where a general tool would
  otherwise be granted.
* Reduce or disable credential caching for sensitive rules, and log sudo use centrally.
data.short_recommendation: Review sudo rules against binary capability, not intent; avoid wildcards.
